title: I'm angry and I can't tell if it's proportionate
blurb: For anger that feels either far too big for what happened, or suspiciously absent.
entry_signals: I should be angry and I'm not
I can't stop thinking about what they said

steps.ask: How activated are you right now, one to ten?

steps.title: Come back to this
steps.say:
Anger this live doesn't get sorted by thinking about it — that just runs the story again, and telling yourself the story keeps pulling the feeling back into your body.

Nothing here is going anywhere. The questions work much better once the spike has passed, and the goal isn't to be calm while furious, it's to catch things earlier next time.

steps.ask: Straight question first: did something happen that would anger a reasonable person?
steps.help: Asked before anything else, because "am I overreacting" is a question people ask most in situations where they aren't.

options.label: Something happened, but I think my reaction was bigger than it

steps.title: Then the anger is doing its job
steps.say:
Anger is information about an injustice. If something happened that would anger a reasonable person, the useful question isn't whether you're allowed to feel it — it's what you want to do with it.

One thing worth checking: are the people who know what happened the same people who'd be able to tell you if you were wrong? If your friends know things about this your partner doesn't, that gap is its own problem.

steps.ask_b: What did it mean about you?
steps.help_b: This is the real question. Most disproportionate anger is carrying a claim about you — that you don't matter, that you're too much, that you'll be left.

steps.ask: Which of these is closest to how the anger feels?

options.label: Hot — I want them to understand how much this hurt
Cold — I want distance, and I think less of them now
Defensive — I need them to see I'm not the bad one here
There isn't much feeling. That's what worries me

steps.ask: If the anger weren't available, what would be underneath it?
steps.help: Anger is often the only feeling that made it through. Cold anger in particular tends to be sitting on hurt that never got registered — and the giveaway is the judgement, not the heat.

steps.ask: Is this the first time, or the tenth?
steps.help: Feelings are usually a compound of many small things rather than the product of one clear cause — which is why a reaction can be entirely proportionate to the pattern and look absurd next to the single incident that triggered it.

options.label: It's happened plenty of times. This one just tipped it

steps.ask: If you raise this, what are you actually arguing for?
steps.help: Be unflattering if that's what's true. Sometimes it's a fix. Sometimes it's for them to see you as the good one, or to keep the upper hand. Those are all real wants, but only the stated one can be agreed to.
cites: Asking What You Are Actually Arguing For

steps.say: The pair worth carrying out of this: what happened, and what you concluded it meant about you. The second one is usually the thing the conversation is really about.
